lesson.title: Copying the Blueprint: How a Cell Duplicates Its DNA
lesson.summary: DNA replication is the process by which a cell makes an exact copy of its entire genome so that each new cell produced by division receives a complete set of genetic instructions.
lesson.body:
Every time a cell divides, whether it is a skin cell replacing itself or a fertilized egg beginning to build an embryo, the two resulting cells need their own full copy of the organism's DNA. Without a way to duplicate DNA first, cell division would simply split one set of chromosomes between two cells, and each daughter cell would end up with only half the genetic information it needs. DNA replication solves this problem: before a cell divides, it copies its DNA so that one full set can go to each daughter cell.

The reason replication is even possible comes directly from the structure of the DNA double helix. Recall that DNA consists of two strands wound around each other, held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: adenine (A) always pairs with thymine (T), and guanine (G) always pairs with cytosine (C). Because the base on one strand always predicts the base across from it, each strand of the helix already contains all the information needed to rebuild its partner. This was one of the most important insights to come out of the discovery of the double helix: the structure itself suggested the copying mechanism.

In broad strokes, replication begins when enzymes unwind and separate the two strands of the double helix at a starting point called an origin of replication, exposing each strand as a template. Other enzymes, most importantly DNA polymerase, then move along each exposed template strand and build a new complementary strand by matching free nucleotides to the template according to the base pairing rules. For example, if a short stretch of template strand reads 3'-TACGGC-5', the newly built partner strand will read 5'-ATGCCG-3', since T pairs with A, A pairs with T, C pairs with G, and so on down the line.

The result is two double helices where there used to be one, and because each new helix is built using an original strand as its template, the copies are (with rare exceptions) faithful reproductions of the original genetic sequence. This has to happen with remarkable speed and accuracy: a human cell must correctly copy billions of base pairs each time it divides. The chapters that follow break this process into its working parts: the enzyme that actually does the building (DNA polymerase), the model that describes how old and new strands end up arranged (semiconservative replication), the asymmetric way the two strands are synthesized (leading and lagging strands and Okazaki fragments), how the cell catches and fixes its own mistakes (proofreading and repair), and a special problem that arises at the very ends of linear chromosomes (telomeres).
